Before a model meets its data, its equations decide which parameters it can determine at all. If
a continuous family of parameter values gives the same prediction for every observable, no data
of these observables, however many and however precise, can tell its members apart. This chapter
finds such families in the model of [chapter 1](guide-model.html) with `symmetryDetection()`, which
calls the Python package [symident](https://dmodverse.github.io/symident/), and removes them before
the fit. The code is `symmetries.R` and the last part of `model.R`.

## Structural identifiability

Write the model as

$$\dot x = f(x, u(t), \theta), \qquad x(t_0) = x_0(\theta), \qquad y = h(x, \theta),$$

with the states $x$, an input $u$, here TNFα, the observables $y$, and the parameters
$\theta \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, rate constants, totals and observation parameters
alike. The prediction is $g(t; \theta) = h(x(t), \theta)$. The model is *locally structurally
identifiable* at $\theta$ if no other $\tilde\theta$ near $\theta$ has the same prediction,
$g(\cdot; \tilde\theta) = g(\cdot; \theta)$. The property is *structural*: it is decided by the
equations alone, as if every observable were measured exactly and continuously in time, and it is
stated for generic $\theta$, for all values outside a set of measure zero. A structural
non-identifiability makes the likelihood exactly flat along a curve in $\Theta$, whatever the data.

## Lie symmetries

A continuous family of parameter values with the same prediction is the orbit of a *Lie symmetry*,
a one-parameter group of transformations $\Phi_\varepsilon$ of $\Theta$ with
$g(t; \Phi_\varepsilon(\theta)) = g(t; \theta)$ for all $t$ and $\varepsilon$ near 0. The group is
determined by its *generator*, the vector field of its velocities at $\varepsilon = 0$,

$$X = \sum_{i=1}^d \xi_i(\theta)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_i}, \qquad
\xi(\theta) = \frac{\partial \Phi_\varepsilon(\theta)}{\partial \varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon = 0},$$

and the orbit through $\theta$ is the integral curve of $X$. A function $I(\theta)$ with
$X(I) = \sum_i \xi_i\, \partial I / \partial \theta_i = 0$ is an *invariant*, constant along every
orbit. The prediction depends on $\theta$ only through the invariants, and the number of
combinations of parameters that the observables determine is $d$ minus the number of independent
generators.

The simplest and in reaction networks the most common symmetries are *scalings*,
$\xi_i(\theta) = w_i \theta_i$ with integer weights $w_i$. Their orbits are
$\theta_i \mapsto e^{w_i \varepsilon} \theta_i$, and on the log scale of the parameters they are
straight lines: $\log \theta_i$ moves by $w_i \varepsilon$. Two examples from the model of
chapter 1:

- An observable `s * (A + B) + off` measures the species only up to the scale `s`. If every
  concentration of a moiety is multiplied by $\lambda$, and every rate constant of a reaction of
  second order in it divided by $\lambda$, the dynamics of the other species are unchanged, and the
  scale divided by $\lambda$ restores the observable. The generator moves the total of the moiety,
  the scales of all its observables and the bimolecular rate constants together.
- TNFα produces active receptors at the rate `uptake * TNF`. Only the product of the uptake and the
  dose enters the equations; with the dose known, the uptake is determined, but the active receptor
  is observed nowhere, and its level trades against the rate constant of IKK activation.

A symmetry need not be a scaling. Merkt, Timmer and Kaschek (2015, Phys Rev E 92:012920) found in
another model of NFκB signalling the transformation $u \mapsto u / (1 - \varepsilon u)$,
$k_0 \mapsto k_0 + \varepsilon$ of an input amplitude $u$ and a constant $k_0$, with the
generator $X = u^2 \partial_u + \partial_{k_0}$. It leaves $k_1 u / (1 + k_0 u) = k_1 / (1/u + k_0)$
unchanged: in $w = 1/u$ it is the translation $w \mapsto w - \varepsilon$, and only the sum
$1/u + k_0$ is determined. A method that looks for scalings alone misses it; symident finds general
generators with rational components.

## Detection

symident decides identifiability from the Taylor series of the prediction in time. The parameters
and the time are added to the states, $z = (x, \theta, t)$ with $\dot\theta = 0$ and $\dot t = 1$,
so that the model is the vector field $F = f\, \partial_x + \partial_t$. Applied to a function
$\varphi(z)$, $F$ gives its rate of change along a solution, and the *Lie derivatives* of the
observables are

$$L_F^0 h = h, \qquad L_F^{k+1} h = F\bigl(L_F^k h\bigr).$$

For an analytic model they fix the prediction at the initial time,

$$g(t; \theta) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{(t - t_0)^k}{k!}\, L_F^k h\bigl(z_0(\theta)\bigr),$$

so two parameter values with the same Lie derivatives at $t_0$ have the same prediction. Collected
up to order $N$ they form $\Psi_N(\theta)$, and its Jacobian is the observability-identifiability
matrix

$$\mathrm{OIM}_N(\theta) = \frac{\partial \Psi_N(\theta)}{\partial \theta}.$$

A generator leaves every Lie derivative unchanged, so its vector $\xi(\theta)$ lies in the kernel
of $\mathrm{OIM}_N(\theta)$; at a generic $\theta$ the kernel consists exactly of these vectors.
The model is identifiable when the matrix has full rank $d$. symident computes the matrix in exact
arithmetic over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$ at a random point, where a rank can only fall below
its generic value, with a small probability that it confirms at further primes and points; it
proves the order $N$ sufficient where it can, and reconstructs the kernel vectors as exact rational
functions $\xi(\theta)$, which it then checks over the rationals.

The cells start at rest: `equilibrate = TRUE` takes the initial state from $f(x, 0, \theta) = 0$,
with the inputs at 0, so the initial values are functions of the parameters and not free. The
conserved moieties leave a family of steady states; `reduceCQ = TRUE` eliminates one species per
moiety and reports the freedom on the totals, the parameters of `Pimpl()`. TNFα is an input state,
`forcings = "TNF"`, which is 0 at rest and set by the event at time 0. The two conditions differ in
the dose, given by `conditions`; a direction is non-identifiable only if it is non-identifiable in
both.

The imaging readouts bleach, $y = \log(s x + o) - \tau t$. symident writes an observable
$a \log h + c$ through $h$, and the bleaching would make $h$ contain $e^{-\tau t}$, a function of
the clock time that a start at rest does not admit. The bleaching rates take no part in a symmetry,
though: in the control the cells rest, the states are constant, and the slope of an imaging readout
is $-\tau$ alone. `symmetries.R` therefore analyses the observables without the bleaching terms.

## The full model

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !detected}
cat("> Results pending: `results/symmetries.rds` of the project is written by `symmetries.R`.\n")
```

```{r symmetries, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = detected}
symmetries <- readRDS("results/symmetries.rds")
symmetries
```

The rank of the observability-identifiability matrix is `r symmetries$rank` of
`r symmetries$dim` coordinates, proven, and the kernel is spanned by ten directions, each proven
over the rationals: nine scalings and one general direction. The ten generators are a basis of the
kernel; symident prints one basis, and a sum of its generators is a symmetry as well. Up to such
sums, the scalings fall into five kinds.

- **Unobserved intermediates.** The active receptor `TNFR`, the IκBα transcript `mIkb`, the A20
  transcript and the A20 protein are measured nowhere, or, A20, only up to a scale. Each enters
  the rest of the network through a product of its level and the rate constant it drives, and a
  level multiplied by $\lambda$ is undone by its production rate multiplied by $\lambda$ and the
  rate it drives divided by $\lambda$: $X_1$ for the receptor (`uptake`, `act_Ikk_by_TNF`), $X_4$
  for the IκBα transcript (`prod_mIkb_by_nNfk`, `prod_Ikb`), $X_6$ for the A20 transcript
  (`build_RnaA20`, `build_A20`). In $X_7$ the A20 protein moves its production, the constant
  `inh_Ikk` of its inhibition of IKK, which enters as `A20 / inh_Ikk`, and the scale of its
  imaging readout.
- **Relative measurements.** Blots and imaging give no absolute amounts. $X_2$ divides the total
  of IKK, and with it every form, by $\lambda$ and multiplies the rate constants of the
  phosphorylations IKK catalyses and the scale of the pIKK blot by $\lambda$; the IKK cycle is
  linear in IKK, so its dynamics only scale.
  NFκB and IκBα scale together: every form multiplied by $\lambda$, the constant of complex
  formation, of second order in them, and the scales of their readouts divided by $\lambda$. The
  printed $X_3$ is this direction plus $X_4$, $X_5$ and $X_6$ and minus $X_7$, which is why it also
  moves the nuclear volume and the production of IκBα.
- **The nuclear volume.** At fixed amounts, a larger nucleus has lower nuclear concentrations. In
  $X_5$ the volume `Vnuc` grows, the nuclear concentrations fall, and the rates that read them, the
  transcription of IκBα and A20 and the formation of the nuclear complex, and the scale of nuclear
  NFκB grow to compensate.
- **A product.** `split_NfkIkb` appears only multiplied by `eta_split_pNfkpIkb` ($X_8$).
- **The ligand.** Nothing in the experiment moves the ligand away from its resting level
  $u = \mathrm{prod\_L} / \mathrm{degrad\_L}$, so only that level enters the prediction, and $X_9$
  multiplies secretion and decay together.

## A general direction

$X_{10}$ is not a scaling. The receptors see TNFα and the ligand together. The dose of TNFα is
known, 0 at rest and 1 after the stimulus, so the rate of receptor activation takes two values,

$$v_0 = \frac{\mathrm{uptake}\; u}{1 + K_R\, u}, \qquad
  v_1 = \frac{\mathrm{uptake}\,(1 + u)}{1 + K_R\,(1 + u)},$$

which three parameters, `uptake`, $K_R$ and the level $u$, produce. $X_{10}$ moves all three and
keeps both values: applied to $v_0$ and to $v_1$ its components cancel. Along an orbit, after a
change of the curve parameter, the level follows $\dot u = -u(1 + u)$, whose solutions take $u$ to

$$u \mapsto \frac{u}{e^{\varepsilon} + (e^{\varepsilon} - 1)\, u},$$

a Möbius transformation of the level, as in the model of Merkt et al.; `K_R` and `uptake` follow
it. The components of the generator are polynomials of degree two, and a search for scalings alone
would not find it. Without the ligand the same holds for the saturation alone: with one dose,
`uptake / (1 + K_R)` is determined, and $K_R$ moves along an affine direction.

## Reduction

`symmetryReduction()` turns the directions into a transformation of the parameters that removes
them. It treats the directions in blocks. For a block of scalings it fixes one coordinate per
direction, a *section* that every orbit meets once. For a general direction it computes its
invariants, rational functions that the generator leaves unchanged, and a section on which the
invariants are new parameters `q_<k>`:

```{r reduction, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = detected}
reduction <- readRDS("results/reduction.rds")
reduction
```

The section of $X_{10}$ is $K_R = 0$, with `prod_L = 1` from $X_9$: there the invariants are
`q_1 = degrad_L` and `q_2 = uptake`, and the receptors are activated at the linear rate
`uptake * (TNF + Lig)` by TNFα and a ligand of level `1 / degrad_L`. The saturation is not
identifiable at all. $K_R = 0$ lies on the boundary of the domain $K_R \ge 0$, a *face*: every
orbit reaches it in the limit, and the prediction there is the limit of the predictions on the
orbit, which are all equal. Two claims of this section are left unproven: that each level set of
the invariants is one orbit, and that the resting state of the model on the face is regular,
which symident did not confirm at random points. `alternatives = TRUE` returns the other valid
sections; here two, which also fix $K_R = 0$ and `prod_L = 1` and pick other coordinates for the
scalings.

## Gauge

A symmetry is removed by fixing one coordinate it moves. Each orbit then meets the fixed values in
one point, and the prediction is the same as on the whole orbit: fixing the coordinate chooses the
units in which the others are measured, it does not change the fit. `model.R` fixes one parameter
per scaling at 1, at 0 on the log scale, and the saturation at the section of the reduction:

```{r gauge}
```

The ten fixed coordinates remove all ten directions if no combination of generators leaves them all
unchanged, that is if the components of the generators on them form a regular matrix. For a
scaling the components are its weights on the log scale; for $X_{10}$ they are its components at a
point of the section, `K_R = 0` and `prod_L = uptake = degrad_L = 1`, divided by the coordinate
where it is on the log scale:

```{r, eval = detected}
point <- c(K_R = 0, prod_L = 1, uptake = 1, degrad_L = 1)
component <- function(X, coordinate) {
  if (identical(X$type, "scaling")) return(as.numeric(X$weights[[coordinate]] %||% 0))
  if (!coordinate %in% names(X$generator)) return(0)
  v <- eval(str2lang(X$generator[[coordinate]]), as.list(point))
  if (coordinate == "K_R") v else v / point[[coordinate]]
}
W <- t(vapply(symmetries$symmetries, function(X)
  vapply(names(gauge), function(cn) component(X, cn), 0), numeric(length(gauge))))
dimnames(W) <- list(paste0("X", seq_len(nrow(W))), names(gauge))
W
det(W)
```

For the scalings the gauge is the one of Oppelt et al.: the totals of NFκB and IKK and the nuclear
volume set the units of the concentrations, and the receptor, the transcripts and A20 are measured
in units of the rates that produce them; the reduction fixes other coordinates of the same
scalings, a different choice of units. With the gauge, the totals are 1: a concentration is a
fraction of the total of its moiety. The fit of [chapter 4](guide-optimization.html) estimates the
remaining `r length(setdiff(getParameters(p), names(gauge)))` parameters. The ligand stays in
the model: whether the data need its level is the question of the profiles of
[chapter 5](guide-profiles.html).
